title: Area V review: Preflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix the five ASEL Tasks of Area V: preflight assessment, flight deck management, engine starting, taxiing with airport signs and lighting, and the before takeoff check. Many join two of them in one real instructing morning, from the records and walkaround to the run-up, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: Your pre-solo learner flies the pattern well. Over her last three lessons you watched her from the walkaround to shutdown: twice you reminded her to drain the left wing sump, and once you prompted the magneto check at the run-up. She asks to solo tomorrow. What does the AIH say about judging her readiness?
options: She is ready: the AIH's solo skills are takeoffs, landings and the pattern, so preflight and run-up prompts do not count
She is ready if she can recite the walkaround and before-takeoff checklists from memory

Not yet: solo readiness is generally judged when you watch her from preflight to engine start to engine shutdown and she performs consistently without instructor assistance, and you still had to prompt her. Tell her exactly what she still needs to show
She is ready: needing two reminders in three lessons is normal, and a first solo is the best way to build her habits
questions.why: The AIH says solo readiness is generally decided when the instructor observes the learner from preflight to engine start to engine shutdown and the learner performs consistently, without need of instructor assistance [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. Two sump reminders and a prompted magneto check mean she is not there yet: every sump is drained during the preflight [[24:47|AFH 2-10]], and the run-up is a test that finds failures on the ground [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. Reciting checklists from memory is no proof either; a checklist can become so automatic that the words no longer trigger the actions [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

questions.q: Reviewing the school trainer's records with your learner, you find two ELT entries: a hard landing last month set it off for 40 minutes, and a ramp bump last week set it off for 35 more. Its 12-month inspection is current and the battery's marked expiration date is next year. Today's lesson is a 120 NM dual cross-country. What applies?
options: The battery must be replaced (or recharged, if rechargeable) before this flight: 40 + 35 = 75 minutes is more than 1 cumulative hour of transmitter use, and a current inspection does not change that
Nothing yet: the battery is due only when its marked expiration date arrives
Nothing: each activation was under 1 hour, so the 1-hour rule is not triggered
Nothing: the ELT rule never applies to training flights
questions.why: 14 CFR 91.207(c) requires ELT batteries to be replaced (or recharged, if rechargeable) when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of their useful life has expired; either one triggers it [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]. Cumulative means the uses add: 40 + 35 = 75 minutes, which is more than 60. The 12-calendar-month inspection is a separate requirement [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. The training exception covers only training operations conducted entirely within 50 NM of the airport where the local flights began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]], and a 120 NM cross-country is not one. Let the learner make the call first, then discuss it [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

questions.q: Your private pilot learner plans to fly himself 200 NM on Sunday evening to a Monday 9:00 job interview. The forecast is VFR but could change. Which plan best fits the AIH approach to external pressure?
options: Plan to lower his ceiling minimum on Sunday if needed, since this trip matters more than an ordinary one
Treat the interview as a minor factor next to weather, since the airplane and the pilot are fine
Fly only with an instructor aboard, since external pressure affects only solo pilots

Build outs before the day: time for a weather stop, a backup airline reservation or a departure early enough to drive, word to the interviewer that he could be delayed, and an overnight kit. The AIH calls managing external pressure the single most important key to risk management, because it can make a pilot ignore every other risk
questions.why: External pressures are influences outside the flight that push to complete it, often at the expense of safety, such as someone waiting at the destination [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]. Managing them is the single most important key to risk management because this category can cause a pilot to ignore all the others, and personal SOPs give the release: time for an extra fuel or weather stop, backup airline reservations or leaving early enough to drive, telling people at the destination about possible delays, and an overnight kit [[25:11|AIH 1-7]]. Lowering a minimum for a specific flight is exactly what the AIH checklist forbids, because then the external pressures decide [[25:206|AIH D-1]].

questions.q: At an airport with airline service, your learner is preflighting on the GA ramp while her friend, waiting to ride along, walks toward a gate marked as a Security Identification Display Area (SIDA) to photograph the airliners. What do you teach your learner?
options: Nothing: airport security is the airport's job, not the pilot's

Passengers move on the ramp only as directed, with an escort if not under her direct supervision. A SIDA needs an airport-issued badge; people without proper ID seen entering one may be reported to the TSA or airport security and fined, and the AIM tells pilots to brief passengers on it
The friend may go in if your learner shows her pilot certificate at the gate
Only the TSA may brief passengers about secured areas, so leave it to them
questions.why: The pilot should caution passengers to move on the surface only as directed, and passengers not under the pilot's direct supervision should have an escort for their safety and ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. A SIDA is a limited access area that requires a badge issued under 49 CFR 1542 [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]]. Pilots or passengers without proper identification observed entering a SIDA may be reported to the TSA or airport security and face civil and criminal fines, and pilots are advised to brief passengers accordingly [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. A pilot certificate is something you show the TSA on request; it is not a SIDA badge [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. Aviation security is on the AIH list of special emphasis items for instructors [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

questions.q: Your learner plans a night cross-country of 1 hour 50 minutes to the first landing at normal cruise, burning 9 gallons per hour with wind included. He has looked in both tanks and confirmed 22 gallons usable. He says, "Legal: with the 30-minute reserve I need 21 gallons." What is your answer?
options: Correct: 22 gallons covers the 21 he needs with a gallon to spare
Legal, because the 45-minute reserve applies only under IFR
Not legal: at night 91.151 requires 45 minutes after the first point of intended landing, so 155 minutes at 9 gph is 23.25 gallons, more than 22
Not legal, because night VFR needs a 60-minute reserve
questions.why: Under 14 CFR 91.151(a), a VFR flight needs enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then, at normal cruising speed, fly at least 30 minutes by day or at least 45 minutes at night [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]]. His math is the day rule: 110 + 30 = 140 minutes, 140/60 x 9 = 21 gallons. At night it is 110 + 45 = 155 minutes, 155/60 x 9 = 23.25 gallons, so 22 gallons is short. Praise the visual check: ramp slope and strut extension change capacity, so the gauges are confirmed by looking in each tank [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

questions.q: Your instrument-rated renter plans a night flight to an unfamiliar airport, ending with an approach. The autopilot failed yesterday. There is no MEL, and the autopilot is not on the equipment list or KOEL, not required by 91.205 and not tied to an AD. He says, "I'll pull and collar the breaker, put an INOP sticker on it, and we're legal." How do you coach him?
options: He is right: a pilot may deactivate and placard an item himself, so once the sticker is on the flight is ready

Deactivation is not preventive maintenance: a person authorized under 43.7 makes the record entry, and a rated pilot or mechanic must decide the item is not a hazard. Even then, legal is only the start. The PHAK says a dead autopilot can take a night approach into an unfamiliar airport from medium to serious risk, so he plans for it or changes the flight
No flight is possible: every installed item must work, so the autopilot must be repaired first
Once it is placarded, nothing more is needed, because an autopilot never changes pilot workload
questions.why: Section 91.213(d) lets a small non-turbine airplane without an MEL fly with an inoperative item that is not required, once it is removed or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative" and a rated pilot or mechanic determines it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. So a repair is not the only path. But AC 91-67A says deactivation is not preventive maintenance, and a person authorized under 43.7 must make the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]; the older PHAK line about a pilot just pulling a breaker [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] is not what to teach. Before flying, weigh night operations, the destination, workload and other human factors [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. The PHAK example is this exact case: a malfunctioning autopilot can be the single factor that takes a night approach into an unfamiliar airport from medium to serious risk [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

questions.q: Your learner will fly a mother and her 20-month-old son in the back seat of a four-seat airplane manufactured in 1981. The front seats have shoulder harnesses; the rear seats have lap belts only. What does 14 CFR say?
options: The boy may ride on his mother's lap in her approved seat because he has not reached his second birthday, and the rear lap belts are enough: a 1981 small airplane needs shoulder harnesses only at the front seats
The boy needs his own seat and belt, because every occupant must have one
No one may ride in back, because every seat in this airplane needs a shoulder harness
The boy may ride on her lap, but she may not sit in back without a shoulder harness
questions.why: Under 91.107(a)(3)(i), a person may be held by an adult in an approved seat if the person held has not reached his or her second birthday and uses no restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. Day VFR requires a safety belt for each occupant 2 years of age or older [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(13)]]. Small airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978 need a shoulder harness for each front seat; only those manufactured after December 12, 1986 need one for all seats [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(14)]]. A 1981 airplane falls between the two dates. Your learner still briefs the belts before takeoff and tells each person to fasten them before moving [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)]].

questions.q: Your private pilot learner's tablet charts and moving-map data expired three weeks ago. Tomorrow she flies VFR to an unfamiliar towered airport under a Class B shelf, with two hot spots on its diagram. She says, "VFR doesn't require current data, so I'm fine." What do you teach?
options: She is right, so the old moving map and the old airport diagram are fine for the whole flight
It is illegal to fly VFR with an outdated GPS database
Old data are fine near Class B as long as the moving map shows no airspace warnings

There is no VFR requirement, but the AIM advises against using a moving map with an outdated database in and around critical airspace and says to verify with current products such as the Chart Supplement and sectional. For the taxi she also needs the current airport diagram, NOTAMs and ATIS, because closures change and may not be marked on the pavement
questions.why: The AIM says databases must be updated for IFR and should be updated for all other operations, there is no requirement to update them for VFR, a moving map with an outdated database is not recommended in and around critical airspace, and pilots using one should verify with current products such as the Chart Supplement or sectional [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. Numerous pilots have flown into airspace they were trying to avoid with an outdated database [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]. On the ground, the Chart Supplement is issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-4]], and a closed runway or taxiway may have no visual indication, so check NOTAMs and the ATIS [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6]]. The 5P check counts database currency as part of the Plane [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

questions.q: On a solo cross-country your learner leaves a 30-lb bag loose on the rear seat (arm 118 in). In turbulence it slides into the baggage area (arm 142 in). The airplane weighs 2,250 lb. How far does the CG move, and what do you teach?
options: About 0.32 in aft (30 x 24 / 2,250). Unsecured baggage can change the CG, so supervise loading and secure every item before engine start
About 3.2 in aft, and 14 CFR 91.525 legally requires the bag to be tied down in a small trainer
None, because the total weight stays the same
About 0.32 in forward, because moving weight aft shifts the CG forward
questions.why: The change in CG equals weight shifted times distance shifted divided by total weight [[22:24|W&B Handbook 2-4]]: 30 x (142 minus 118) = 720 lb-in, and 720 / 2,250 = 0.32 in, aft because the weight moved aft. Total weight does not change, but the CG still moves. The AFH says the pilot supervises baggage loading because unsecured or improperly loaded baggage may affect the CG [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Section 91.525 is in Part 91 subpart F, which governs large and turbine-powered multiengine airplanes and fractional ownership aircraft [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]], so its cargo list is a teaching standard for a trainer, not a binding rule.

questions.q: Your private pilot learner is about to take his father on his first ride in a chocked trainer. In his briefing he says, "After I start, Dad, hop out and pull the chocks, then climb back in." What do you teach?
options: Fine, as long as his father walks out in front of the wing where the pilot can see him
Fine, because the rotating beacon will warn his father the engine is running
Fine once the parking brake is set, because the airplane cannot move

Change the plan. Once it turns, the propeller is nearly invisible, and people walking or reaching into the arc after a start to pull chocks or reach the cabin have been seriously injured and killed. Chocks are approached only from behind the propeller with the throttle at idle, never from the front or side. Brief propeller blade avoidance, and have passengers board and leave only with the engine stopped
questions.why: The AFH warns that the propeller is nearly invisible after start and that serious injuries and fatalities have occurred when people who have just started an engine walk or reach into the propeller arc to remove chocks or reach the cabin; chocks are approached only from the rear of the propeller with the throttle at idle, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Passengers move on the ramp only as directed [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Propeller blade avoidance is one of the ACS AI.V.B S2 briefing items, and the start itself begins with a clear area and a CLEAR call that is answered [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. A set brake keeps the airplane still but does nothing about the blade.

questions.q: On a cold morning the line crew gives your learner a GPU start because the battery is weak. After the cord is pulled and she starts to taxi, the ammeter stays pegged high and does not come down, the panel lights dim, and the headset whines. She says the battery is just recharging after the GPU start. What do you teach?
options: These are the signs of a starter that stayed engaged: shut down now, and no flight until the cause is found and fixed. A starter relay stuck on can overload and overheat the electrical system and destroy the starter drive
She is right: after a GPU start the ammeter always reads very high until the run-up
Continue to the run-up and recheck the ammeter there before deciding
Turn off the radios to stop the whine and continue the taxi
questions.why: The AFH says a starter that stays engaged after start shows as a continuous, very high current draw on the ammeter, and the engine should be shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. AC 91-55A lists low voltage, high ammeter readings, dimming lights and excessive radio noise as signs of prolonged starter running; the engine should be shut down and no further flight attempted until the cause is found and repaired, because a relay stuck on can overload the electrical system, overheat components and destroy the starter drive [[18:1|AC 91-55A]]. A GPU is useful in cold weather, but the manufacturer's procedure governs the start [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]; it does not explain away a reading that stays pegged with dim lights.

questions.q: At 20 degrees F your learner cranks the school trainer's unheated engine for 45 seconds, pauses 10 seconds, and cranks again until she smells burning insulation. A friend on the ramp offers to hand prop it. Which coaching fits the AFH?
options: Accept the hand prop, since it saves the starter from more heat

Stop. Cranking should not run past 30 seconds without a cool-down of 30 seconds to 1 minute, or longer if the POH says, and the smell suggests she exceeded it. Preheat when temperatures approach and fall below freezing, and after repeated failed starts get advice from a qualified person. A starter-equipped airplane that will not start is a maintenance item, not a hand propping job
Keep cranking in short bursts, because a starter cannot overheat in cold weather
Give it several extra primer strokes, since a cold engine cannot be overprimed
questions.why: The AFH says to avoid continuous starter operation longer than 30 seconds without a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute (some POHs say longer), that a burning insulation smell may mean the cranking limit was exceeded, and that after repeated unsuccessful attempts the pilot should seek advice from a qualified person [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. It also calls for preheat as temperatures approach and fall below freezing [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. On a starter-equipped airplane the starter should work if the airplane is airworthy, and if not a certificated mechanic should be called [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Overpriming is a hazard, so follow the airplane's priming instructions [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

questions.q: Your learner's tiedown leaves the tail pointed into an open hangar where a mechanic is working, with loose gravel under the propeller. She plans to start there, then add a burst of power to roll out over a small bump. What do you teach?
options: Start there: the mechanic will hear the engine and step away

Move the airplane by hand to a clear, firm spot first: check behind before every start, because prop thrust can throw objects at high speed, and keep the propeller away from gravel. Once rolling, retard the throttle right away and check the brakes
Start there, but never add power to start moving, so the blast stays small
Start there: positioning matters only for the run-up, not for the start
questions.why: Before start the pilot checks that the area is clear and checks what is behind the airplane as standard practice, because propeller thrust can accelerate objects to substantial velocities, damaging property and injuring people [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. The airplane should be where the propeller will not stir up gravel or dust [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. ACS AI.V.C S1 asks you to position the airplane considering structures, nearby persons and property. More power may be needed to start moving, but the throttle is retarded as soon as the airplane moves, and the brakes are tested right away [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], so the burst is not the problem; the spot is.

questions.q: During the shutdown check, your learner turns the ignition switch to OFF at idle and the engine keeps running. She quickly turns it back to BOTH. What does this mean, and what do you teach?
options: A magneto is not grounded, as with a broken ground wire, so the engine could fire if the propeller is moved even with the switch OFF. Stop it with the mixture at idle cutoff, treat the propeller as live, warn others, and have a qualified AMT check it
The master switch is still on; turning it off will stop the engine and make the propeller safe
Normal at idle, because magnetos keep firing for a few seconds after OFF
Turn the key to START briefly to reset the magnetos, then try OFF again
questions.why: The AFH shutdown list includes a momentary check for proper magneto grounding in the OFF position at idle [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. A magneto makes its own current, independent of the airplane's electrical system [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]], so the master switch cannot stop it. If the ground wire between a magneto and the switch is broken, the engine could start with the switch OFF when the propeller is moved, and the only way to stop it is the mixture at idle cutoff, then a check by a qualified AMT [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Teach the AFH rule for any time a propeller is touched: always assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: Your learner taxis on a taxiway heading 090 toward the run-up pad in a nosewheel trainer. The wind is 200 at 15 knots. How should she hold the controls, and which way should she point the airplane for the run-up?
options: Yoke turned right and held back, then run up facing 090
Yoke turned right and pushed forward, then run up facing about 020 so the wind blows from behind
Yoke turned left (right aileron down) and pushed forward (elevator down) for a right quartering tailwind; at the pad, head as nearly as possible into the wind, toward about 200
Controls neutral, because ailerons and elevator do nothing at taxi speed, then any heading for the run-up
questions.why: Wind from 200 on a 090 heading is 110 degrees right of the nose, so it strikes from the right rear: a quartering tailwind. With a quartering tailwind, hold the elevator DOWN and the upwind aileron DOWN, so the wind cannot get under the tail and wing [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. The upwind wing is the right one, and right aileron down means yoke left. Neutral controls are for no-wind taxiing [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. For the run-up, head the airplane as nearly as possible into the wind to limit cylinder overheating, then let it roll forward slightly to align the nosewheel [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

questions.q: On a night dual lesson your learner taxis with the taxi light, landing light and strobes all on. She stops at the run-up pad facing another airplane waiting there, and later is told to line up and wait. Which light plan fits the AIM?
options: Keep every light on the whole time, because more light is always safer
At the pad, taxi light off while stopped, and strobes off if they affect the other pilot; entering to line up and wait, all lights except the landing light, which comes on with the takeoff clearance
Turn the beacon and position lights off at the pad to save the battery, then turn everything on for takeoff
Turn the landing light on as she enters the runway to line up and wait, since that makes her most visible
questions.why: The AIM suggests the taxi light on when moving or about to move and off when stopped or yielding, and strobes off during taxi if they would affect other pilots or ground personnel [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24e]]. When entering the departure runway for takeoff or to line up and wait, all lights except the landing lights should be on; landing lights go on with the takeoff clearance, or at the start of the roll at a nontowered field [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24g]]. Position lights must be lit from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]], so turning them off is not an option. Some landing lights can overheat or drain the electrical system in long taxi use [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

questions.q: Right after a normal start, with oil pressure up in 20 seconds, your learner adds power to roll out of the tiedown, retards the throttle and presses the left brake to check it. The pedal goes soft and the airplane keeps rolling toward a parked airplane. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Shut the engine down immediately; unsatisfactory braking found in the brake check is exactly that case
Add power and steer away with the rudder, then troubleshoot the brake at the run-up
Pump the brake and finish the taxi using the right brake alone
Turn the yoke hard right to steer away with the ailerons
questions.why: The brakes are tested as soon as the airplane moves: retard the throttle and press one side, then the other, and if braking performance is unsatisfactory, the engine should be shut down immediately [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. More power only adds speed toward the parked airplane. The ailerons are not steering devices on the ground [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. This is one reason brakes are held during the start too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Brief on the ground who stops the airplane, and how, if you take the controls.

questions.q: On an instrument student's departure in fog with RVR below 1,200 ft, she loses track of her position on a long taxi route and is not sure whether she has passed taxiway C. A runway lies somewhere ahead, and the tower cannot see the airplane. What do you teach?
options: Stop, but not on a runway, and tell the controller at the first sign of disorientation; ask for progressive taxi, and use the pink geographic position markings to report where she is
Keep rolling slowly and look for the next sign, because stopping blocks other traffic
Continue to the runway ahead, stop there where the lights are better, and call the tower
Study the moving map while continuing the taxi, then report position once sure
questions.why: In low visibility the tower may not be able to see the airplane, so pilots must notify the controller at the first indication of becoming disoriented [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]]. AC 91-73B says that whenever a pilot is uncertain of position, do not stop on a runway; stop the aircraft, advise ATC immediately, and request progressive taxi if needed, and heads-down tasks are done only while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g]]. Progressive taxi gives step-by-step routing when confusion exists [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b]]. Geographic position markings, a pink circle with a designation, sit left of the centerline on low visibility taxi routes to identify a taxiing aircraft's location [[33:149|AIM 2-3-4g]].

questions.q: At a nontowered airport, a twin larger than your learner's trainer makes a touch-and-go on Runway 18 in a light crosswind. Thirty seconds later your learner, holding short, wants to taxi on and depart. Which plan fits the AIM and PHAK?
options: Go now: vortices blow off the runway within seconds in any crosswind
Go now but rotate early, the same fix as departing behind a departing larger aircraft
Wait for ATC's 3-minute interval, which may not be waived

Wait at least 2 minutes after the touch-and-go, because vortices settle and move along the runway and a light crosswind can hold the upwind one in the touchdown zone. Then scan final, enter with lights on, and turn the landing light on as the roll starts
questions.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, vortices settle and move laterally near the ground, so the hazard may stay along the runway, especially in light quartering wind; the AIM says to ensure at least 2 minutes have elapsed before your takeoff [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can keep the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone for a time [[1:107|PHAK 5-10]]. Rotating early is the procedure for following a larger aircraft's takeoff, not its touch-and-go. There is no tower here to set an interval. At a nontowered field, taxi onto the runway only when it is clear and no one is on final [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]], with lights on and the landing light on as the takeoff roll begins [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

questions.q: Your commercial learner moves up to an airplane with a constant-speed propeller and a carburetor. At the run-up she pulls carburetor heat, watches the tachometer, sees no change and calls the check good. What do you teach?
options: She is right: no rpm change means the carburetor has no ice
Carburetor heat is not checked on constant-speed propeller airplanes

With a constant-speed propeller, watch manifold pressure: a drop that stays means no ice, a drop then a gradual rise means ice was present. Also cycle the propeller, which checks the system and brings warm oil into the governor; skipping it risks an overspeed on takeoff
Watch only the tachometer for a gradual rise; that is the ice sign in every airplane
questions.why: The PHAK says carburetor heat is checked during the run-up. With a fixed-pitch propeller, ice shows as an rpm drop followed by a gradual rise; with a constant-speed propeller, it shows as a drop in manifold pressure followed by a gradual increase [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. So a learner moving to a constant-speed airplane has to change which gauge she reads. The AFH has the propeller cycled to confirm it works and to circulate warm oil through the governor, because without it the engine may overspeed on takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

questions.q: Your instrument student starts the engine, taxis 300 feet and begins the run-up 2 minutes after start, planning an IFR departure into a 600-ft overcast. Suction reads below the POH range and the heading indicator is drifting. She wants to go. What do you teach?
options: Go: suction always comes up in the climb

Do not depart into IMC like this. The IFH allows 5 minutes after start for the gyros to spin up, and the AFH says a hasty taxi and run-up keeps mechanical gyros from indicating properly, so an IMC departure is unadvisable. If suction stays below the POH range after the gyros have had time, the attitude and heading indicators may not be reliable
Go, and use the attitude indicator as the primary reference until the heading indicator settles
Tap the suction gauge; if the needle moves, the system is fine
questions.why: The IFH says to allow 5 minutes after start for the heading indicator gyro to spin up [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The AFH says gyros need adequate time to spool up, and a hasty taxi and run-up does not allow them to indicate properly, so a departure into IMC is unadvisable; vacuum values come from the AFM/POH [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. When suction is low, the attitude and heading indicators may not provide reliable information [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]], so leaning on the attitude indicator does not fix it. The no-go call is the PIC's to make [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

questions.q: Your learner worked the takeoff chart for a solo flight at 2,000 lb and found a ground roll of 900 ft. At the airplane, a friend asks to come along, bringing the weight to 2,200 lb. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, what should she expect, and what does she do?
options: About 10 percent longer, about 990 ft, so no recheck is needed
No change: weight affects the climb, not the takeoff roll
About 19 percent shorter, since the extra weight improves traction

At least 21 percent longer, about 1,089 ft or more, since 2,200 lb is 10 percent heavier. Rework the POH chart for the new weight and brief the friend before start, because the PIC must know the takeoff distance for this flight
questions.why: 2,200 / 2,000 = 1.10, a 10 percent increase. The PHAK says a 10 percent increase in takeoff gross weight causes at least a 21 percent increase in takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]: 900 x 1.21 = 1,089 ft or more. The 19 percent figure is the effect of a headwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed, not weight [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Before any flight the PIC must know runway lengths and the takeoff distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]], and takeoffs grow more hazardous as calculated performance approaches the runway available [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. A new passenger also means a new briefing and loading the pilot supervises [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
